families.s: HSE workplace, site and transport-lighting guidance
families.t: sufficient task lighting, glare, shadows, maintenance, emergency lighting and vehicle-route visibility
f: Every workplace must have suitable and sufficient lighting.
Roads, manoeuvring areas, yards and pedestrian areas need lighting adequate for safe movement.
Lighting equipment should be maintained and covers kept clean.
More detailed visual tasks generally require higher light levels.
Poor lighting can contribute to eyestrain, headache, reduced concentration and accidents.
Shadows can obscure tools, edges, stairways and other hazards and may require supplementary lighting.
Emergency lighting is required where primary-light failure would create a health or safety risk.
Lighting should be positioned to avoid glare, confusion and dangerous changes between bright and dark areas.
families.g: Lighting adequacy depends on the task, contrast, colour rendering, glare, shadows, natural light, maintenance, emergency needs, weather and the visual capability of workers.

families.s: HSE driving and riding safely for work guidance
families.t: journey, driver or rider, vehicle, fatigue, competence, health, contractor and incident-management controls
f: Health and safety law applies to driving or riding for work in the same way as other work activities.
Risk assessment should cover the journey, the driver or rider and the vehicle.
Journey planning should consider necessity, route, schedule, weather, breaks and welfare access.
Employers must assess driver competence, capability, licensing, experience and training needs.
Fatigue reduces reaction time, vigilance, concentration and decision quality.
Fitness, eyesight, medication, posture, stress and mental health can affect driving safety.
Vehicles used for work must be suitable, safely maintained and provided with appropriate safety aids.
Incidents and near misses should be reported, investigated and used to improve controls.
families.g: Driving-for-work risk depends on journey necessity and route, schedule and fatigue, weather, driver health and competence, vehicle condition, load, telematics and organisational pressure.

families.s: HSE workplace vehicle-reversing prevention and control guidance
families.t: elimination or minimisation of reversing, marked zones, visibility, signallers, alarms, cameras and site rules
f: A substantial proportion of workplace-transport deaths occur during reversing.
The most effective control is to remove the need for reversing, for example through one-way systems.
Where reversing cannot be eliminated, its frequency and distance should be minimised.
Reversing areas should be planned, clearly marked and kept clear of people who do not need to be there.
Visiting drivers should receive information about site layout and rules.
Safe reversing requires combined controls addressing site, driver and vehicle rather than reliance on one measure.
Blind-spot mirrors, alarms, cameras or proximity systems may support reversing controls where appropriate.
A trained signaller may be used where necessary, with a safe system keeping the signaller out of danger.
families.g: Reversing risk depends on site layout, visibility and blind spots, vehicle size, pedestrian presence, lighting, alarm effectiveness, signaller positioning, driver familiarity and enforcement.

families.s: HSE pedestrian and workplace-vehicle segregation guidance
families.t: separate routes, barriers, crossings, doors, visibility, induction and control of shared areas
f: Roadways and footpaths should be separated wherever possible.
Vehicle routes must be kept sufficiently far from pedestrian doors, gates and routes to avoid danger.
Barriers, guard rails, raised kerbs and markings can separate vehicles from pedestrian areas.
Crossing points should provide clear sight lines, markings, signs and dropped kerbs where appropriate.
Separate doors should be provided for vehicles and pedestrians where possible.
Pedestrian walkways and cycleways should be clearly identified and separated from vehicle routes.
Site planning should map how vehicles and people move and identify points of interaction.
Staff, contractors and visitors need induction and information about routes and restricted areas.
families.g: Segregation effectiveness depends on route design, vehicle and pedestrian volumes, desire lines, crossings, barriers, visibility, shift patterns, visitor behaviour and enforcement.

families.s: HSE mobile-elevating-work-platform selection and safe-use guidance
families.t: selection, entrapment, overturning, falls, collision, rescue, competence, inspection and thorough examination
f: Major MEWP hazards include entrapment, overturning, falls and collision.
The MEWP selected must be suitable for the job and site conditions.
Firm level ground, correctly deployed outriggers and appropriate spreader plates may be required.
A rescue plan should be prepared and practised, with someone able to operate ground controls.
Operators need recognised training plus familiarisation with the specific make and model.
Daily checks, regular inspection, servicing and prompt defect correction are required.
A MEWP used to lift people must normally receive thorough examination at least every six months or under a competent-person scheme.
Secondary guarding must be selected for the specific entrapment risk and its limitations understood.
families.g: MEWP risk depends on machine type and reach, ground and outriggers, overhead obstructions, load, weather, traffic, rescue readiness, inspection condition and operator competence.

families.s: HSE crane and construction lifting-operation guidance
families.t: competent planning, supervision, safe execution, crane stability, accessories, signalling, examination and exclusion controls
f: Every lifting operation must be properly planned by a competent person.
Lifting operations must be appropriately supervised and carried out safely.
Cranes and lifting accessories must have adequate strength and be tested and examined as required.
Crane operators, slingers and people directing lifts must be trained and competent.
Crane collapse can expose both on-site and off-site people to multiple-fatality risk.
Safe crane use requires planning, a safe system, supervision and thorough examination.
Equipment that lifts people requires enhanced design, maintenance, inspection and examination controls.
Lifting people introduces collision, overturning and fall hazards that must be specifically assessed.
families.g: Crane and lifting risk depends on load and radius, crane configuration and stability, ground, wind, accessories, signalling, exclusion zones, nearby structures and competence.

families.s: HSE storage and warehousing health-and-safety guidance
families.t: warehouse transport, storage, manual handling, falls, racking, work equipment and worker coordination
f: Storage and warehousing work presents significant injury and ill-health risks.
Warehouse risk management must cover employees and visiting workers such as hauliers and couriers.
Moving vehicles are a major cause of warehouse injury.
Manual handling is a major warehouse risk requiring assessment and control.
Storage layout and work organisation should be managed to prevent people being struck by goods or equipment.
Warehouse risk assessment should focus on significant hazards and proportionate controls.
Purpose-built MEWPs are generally preferable to non-integrated forklift cages for planned work at height.
Employers must coordinate transport, equipment and pedestrian controls across warehouse activities.
families.g: Warehouse risk depends on racking and load stability, vehicle-pedestrian interaction, picking method, manual handling, work at height, housekeeping, contractors and supervision.

families.s: HSE ports and docks workplace-transport and dangerous-goods guidance
families.t: dock traffic, ramps, quay edges, cargo areas, unfamiliar drivers, lifting, containers and dangerous-goods coordination
f: Common port risks include workplace transport, lifting operations, freight containers and work at height.
Ports contain drivers from multiple employers and members of the public who may be unfamiliar with the dock.
Dock hazards include vehicle and plant movement, loading, unsecured loads and trailer coupling.
Vehicle and pedestrian segregation is required on ro-ro bridges, ramps, quays and cargo areas.
Reversing near open quay edges and vehicles with restricted visibility require specific controls.
Dangerous Goods in Harbour Areas Regulations require measures to reduce major-accident risk.
Port dangerous-goods arrangements must coordinate ship and shore activities.
Emergency planning and dutyholder responsibilities must reflect the dangerous goods passing through the harbour area.
families.g: Port risk depends on vessel and cargo operations, traffic mix, quay and ramp layout, visibility, weather and tides, load security, dangerous goods and multi-employer coordination.

families.s: HSE event planning, management and incident-response guidance
families.t: organiser duties, competent staffing, coordination, site operation, monitoring, first aid, emergency access and post-event review
f: Event organisers retain responsibility for overall event health and safety so far as reasonably practicable.
Event arrangements must control risks during setup, operation and breakdown.
Organisers must coordinate contractors and other work activities.
Staff need relevant information and competence for their safety roles.
Once site activity begins, management and monitoring of real operations must replace reliance on paperwork alone.
Emergency plans should cover emergency-service liaison, evacuation, crowd and traffic management and incident control.
First-aid and medical needs assessments should consider workers and the visiting public.
Safety arrangements should be reviewed after the event and after significant incidents or changes.
families.g: Event risk depends on venue and activity, attendance, contractors, temporary structures, weather, transport, emergency access, public profile, medical provision and operational monitoring.

families.s: HSE crowd-safety assessment and control guidance
families.t: crowd dynamics, capacity, entry, circulation, exit, barriers, stewarding, monitoring and emergency response
f: Crowd safety requires clear roles, cooperation, risk assessment, controls, monitoring and emergency planning.
Risk assessment must consider crowd movement and behaviour during arrival, entry, circulation, exit and dispersal.
Crowd hazards include surging, crushing, falls, trampling, poor routes, inadequate exits and temporary-structure failure.
Organisers should establish safe capacity and prepare a crowd-management plan.
Entry, circulation and exit controls can combine queuing systems, signs, barriers and stewarding.
Security searching must not create dangerous overcrowding or block emergency access.
Routes should be kept free of pinch points and controls should anticipate crowd surges and movement between attractions.
The organiser retains overall public-safety responsibility even when crowd functions are contracted.
families.g: Crowd risk depends on attendance and audience profile, density and flow, venue geometry, barriers, stewarding, weather, transport timing, behaviour, communications and emergency capacity.
